objective: In a position-time graph, positive slope indicates forward movement, negative slope indicates backward movement, steeper slope means faster motion, and a horizontal line means the object is stationary (zero velocity).；In a position-time graph, the sign of the position change indicates direction of motion, not acceleration or deceleration.；In a velocity-time graph, positive slope means speeding up in the positive direction or slowing down in the negative direction; zero slope means constant velocity.

learningGoals.statement: Interpret position-time graphs: slope indicates velocity (positive/negative/zero), direction, and speed.
Interpret velocity-time graphs: slope indicates acceleration, area under curve indicates displacement.
Interpret acceleration-time graphs: area under curve indicates change in velocity, constant acceleration focus.
Apply vector scale diagrams: appropriate scaling, tip-to-tail addition, distinguish speed vs velocity.

knowledgeNodes.name: Position-Time Graph Interpretation
knowledgeNodes.definition: A position-time graph plots position on the y-axis versus time on the x-axis. The slope of the line represents velocity: positive slope = forward motion, negative slope = backward motion, steeper slope = faster speed, horizontal line = stationary. The sign of position change indicates direction, not acceleration.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.

knowledgeNodes.name: Velocity-Time Graph Interpretation
knowledgeNodes.definition: A velocity-time graph plots velocity on the y-axis versus time on the x-axis. The slope represents acceleration: positive slope = speeding up in positive direction or slowing down in negative direction; zero slope = constant velocity. The area under the curve equals total displacement.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.

knowledgeNodes.name: Acceleration-Time Graph Interpretation
knowledgeNodes.definition: An acceleration-time graph plots acceleration on the y-axis versus time on the x-axis. Positive values indicate positive acceleration, negative values indicate negative acceleration. The area under the curve equals the change in velocity over that time interval. Only constant acceleration graphs are assessed in this course.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.

knowledgeNodes.name: Vector Scale Diagrams
knowledgeNodes.definition: Vector scale diagrams must be scaled appropriately: smaller scale for large distances (e.g., city maps), larger scale for small objects (e.g., ants). Vectors are added using the tip-to-tail method. Average speed is scalar; average velocity is vector and includes direction.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: Investigate uniform and non-uniform linear motion in qualitative and quantitative terms, and solve related problems.

reteachModules.trigger: Student chooses 'decelerating' or 'moving forward' when negative slope on PT graph
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student incorrectly thinks a negative slope on a position-time graph always means deceleration, when it actually indicates direction of motion (backwards).

miniLesson.explain: In a position-time graph, the slope represents velocity, a vector that includes direction. Positive slope means forward motion, negative slope means backward motion. The steepness indicates speed: steeper slope = faster motion, horizontal line = stationary. The sign of the slope tells direction, not whether the object is speeding up or slowing down. Deceleration would be indicated by a change in slope (curve) or a slope approaching zero, not simply a negative slope.
miniLesson.example: Consider a car whose position decreases from 10 m to 0 m over 5 seconds. The slope is (0 m - 10 m)/(5 s) = -2 m/s. This negative velocity means the car moves backward at 2 m/s. It is not necessarily decelerating; it could be moving backward at constant speed. Deceleration while moving forward would show a positive slope that decreases over time (curved downward).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: In position-time graphs, slope sign = direction of motion. Negative slope = moving backward. Don't confuse with deceleration. Look for curved lines to spot acceleration.

guidedPractice.prompt: A position-time graph shows a straight line going downwards. What does the negative slope tell you about the object's motion?
A student says that a negative slope on a position-time graph means the object is decelerating. Is this correct? Explain.
guidedPractice.answer: No. A negative slope means the object is moving in the negative direction (backward), not that it is slowing down. Deceleration would be shown by a changing slope (curving), not a constant negative slope. A constant negative slope indicates constant velocity backward.

guidedPractice.prompt: Given a position-time graph with a straight line sloping downward from position +20 m to -10 m in 10 seconds. Calculate the velocity and describe the motion. Is the object decelerating? Why or why not?
guidedPractice.answer: Velocity = change in position / time = (-10 m - 20 m) / 10 s = -30 m / 10 s = -3 m/s. The object is moving backward at a constant speed of 3 m/s. It is not decelerating because the slope is constant (straight line), meaning zero acceleration. Deceleration would require a curved graph (changing slope).

reteachModules.trigger: The student answers that the area under a velocity-time graph represents 'total distance traveled' instead of 'displacement'.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often think the area under a velocity-time graph gives the total distance traveled, but it actually gives displacement. The difference is that displacement accounts for direction (sign), while distance is the sum of absolute areas.

miniLesson.explain: In a velocity-time graph, the area between the curve and the time axis represents displacement. When velocity is positive, area is positive; when velocity is negative, area is negative. The net area (sum of positive and negative areas) gives displacement, not the total distance. For example, if you walk forward 10 m and then back 5 m, your displacement is 5 m but distance traveled is 15 m.
miniLesson.example: Consider a velocity-time graph: from t=0 to t=5 s, v=2 m/s (positive), area = 10 m; from t=5 to t=10 s, v=-1 m/s (negative), area = -5 m. Net area = 5 m, which is displacement. Distance = 10 + 5 = 15 m.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Area under VT = displacement (direction matters) => Net area = final position - initial position. Think of a bank account: deposits (positive velocity) and withdrawals (negative velocity); balance is net, not total deposits.

guidedPractice.prompt: The velocity-time graph shows a constant velocity of 3 m/s for 4 seconds. What is the displacement?
A velocity-time graph has a rectangle from 0 to 3 s at v = 4 m/s and from 3 to 5 s at v = -2 m/s. What is the displacement?
guidedPractice.answer: 8 m (positive area: 4×3 = 12 m; negative area: -2×2 = -4 m; net: 12 + (-4) = 8 m)

guidedPractice.prompt: A velocity-time graph: 0-2 s: v=2 m/s (constant), 2-4 s: v increases linearly from 2 to 6 m/s, 4-6 s: v=6 m/s constant. Find displacement.

reteachModules.trigger: When a student chooses 'acceleration' or 'final velocity' as the meaning of the area under an acceleration-time graph.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Student thinks the area under an acceleration-time graph represents the acceleration value itself or the final velocity, rather than the change in velocity.

miniLesson.explain: The area under an acceleration-time graph equals the change in velocity over that time interval, not the acceleration itself (which is the y-value) nor the final velocity (which depends on initial velocity). For constant acceleration, area = acceleration × time = Δv.
miniLesson.example: Consider a constant acceleration of 2 m/s² for 5 s. The area under the graph is a rectangle: area = 2 × 5 = 10 m/s. This means the velocity changes by 10 m/s. If the initial velocity is 0, the final velocity is 10 m/s, but the area only gives the change, not the final velocity itself.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Area under a-t graph = Δv. Think: 'acceleration × time = velocity change'. So the area tells you how much velocity changed, not the velocity itself.

guidedPractice.prompt: What does the area under an acceleration-time graph represent?
A car accelerates from rest at 3 m/s² for 4 s. Calculate the area under the acceleration-time graph and state what it represents.
guidedPractice.answer: Area = 3 × 4 = 12 m/s. This represents the change in velocity, so the car's velocity after 4 s is 12 m/s (since initial was 0).

guidedPractice.prompt: Object A has a constant acceleration of 5 m/s² for 2 s. Object B has a constant acceleration of 2 m/s² for 5 s. Compare the areas under their acceleration-time graphs and the accelerations. What does this tell you about the meaning of the area?
guidedPractice.answer: Both areas are 10 m/s (5×2 = 10, 2×5 = 10), so the change in velocity is the same. But accelerations are different (5 m/s² vs 2 m/s²). This shows that area gives Δv, not acceleration.

reteachModules.trigger: Student chooses 'acceleration' as meaning of position-time graph slope
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: The student confuses the slope of a position-time graph with acceleration, when it actually represents velocity.

miniLesson.explain: The slope of a position-time graph represents velocity, not acceleration. Velocity is the rate of change of position, so a steeper slope means faster motion, a positive slope means forward motion, a negative slope means backward motion, and a horizontal line means zero velocity (stationary). Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so it is represented by the slope of a velocity-time graph, not a position-time graph.
miniLesson.example: Consider a car moving forward at a constant speed of 10 m/s. The position-time graph is a straight line with a positive slope of 10 m/s. The slope indicates velocity (10 m/s), not acceleration (which is 0 since speed is constant).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: 'Slope of Position is Velocity (SPV)'. To get acceleration, you need the slope of a Velocity-Time graph.

guidedPractice.prompt: What does the slope of a position-time graph represent?
A position-time graph shows a straight line from (0 s, 2 m) to (5 s, 12 m). Calculate the slope. What does it represent?
guidedPractice.answer: Slope = (12-2)/(5-0) = 10/5 = 2 m/s. It represents velocity (2 m/s forward).

guidedPractice.prompt: An object moves forward for 3 seconds at 4 m/s, then backward for 2 seconds at 2 m/s. Sketch its position-time graph and determine the slope during each segment. What does each slope represent?
guidedPractice.answer: First segment: slope = 4 m/s (velocity forward). Second segment: slope = -2 m/s (velocity backward). The slopes represent velocities, not accelerations.

questions.stem: A velocity-time graph shows a positive velocity of 5 m/s for 4 seconds, then a negative velocity of 3 m/s for 2 seconds. What does the total area (sum of positive and negative areas) represent?
A car moves forward at 10 m/s for 3 seconds, then reverses at 4 m/s for 2 seconds. Calculate the car's displacement and total distance traveled. Show your work.
questions.rubric: Correctly calculates displacement = (10 m/s × 3 s) + (-4 m/s × 2 s) = 30 m - 8 m = 22 m. Correctly calculates distance = (10 m/s × 3 s) + (4 m/s × 2 s) = 30 m + 8 m = 38 m. Must show area calculations and distinguish between net and total area.

retestCards.passRule: Answer both questions correctly: Q1 must select 'The displacement', Q2 must correctly calculate both displacement (22 m) and distance (38 m) with proper reasoning showing area calculations and distinction between net and total area.

questions.stem: What does the area under an acceleration-time graph represent?
A cart experiences a constant acceleration of 4 m/s² for 3 s. Calculate the area under the acceleration-time graph and explain what this value represents.
questions.rubric: Correct calculation (12 m/s) AND explains it represents change in velocity (Δv), not final velocity or acceleration.

retestCards.passRule: Must answer Q1 correctly and provide a complete correct response for Q2 (correct calculation and correct interpretation).

questions.stem: A position-time graph is shown for a car moving in a straight line. The graph is a straight line with a positive slope. What physical quantity does the slope of this graph represent?

Consider the position-time graph of an object that is moving forward and then backward. The slope of each segment is calculated. Explain why the slope of the position-time graph is not a measure of acceleration, and what it actually represents.
questions.rubric: The student must state that slope represents velocity (rate of change of position). They must explain that acceleration is the slope of a velocity-time graph, not a position-time graph. A full answer may note that a positive slope means forward motion, negative slope backward, and steeper slope means faster speed.

cards.successCriteria: Student identifies that negative slope means moving backward (direction), not deceleration.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Position-time graph interpretation directly addresses understanding of uniform linear motion.
cards.commonMisconception: Negative slope on a position-time graph is often misinterpreted as deceleration rather than motion in the negative direction.

cards.question: What does the slope of a position-time graph represent?
cards.diagnosis: Check if student confuses slope of PT graph with acceleration.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
The slope of a position-time graph gives velocity, not acceleration. Acceleration is the slope of a velocity-time graph.
Displacement is the difference between final and initial positions, not the slope.
Slope gives velocity (vector), not just speed (scalar). Velocity includes direction.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies slope as velocity.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Understanding slope meaning is fundamental to interpreting position-time graphs.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often think slope of position-time graph gives acceleration because it relates to change in position.

cards.question: The velocity-time graph below shows the motion of an object. What does the area under the curve represent?
cards.diagnosis: Check if student confuses displacement (vector) with distance (scalar) when interpreting VT graph area.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
Area gives displacement (vector) which accounts for direction. Distance would be the absolute sum of areas.
Acceleration is the slope of the VT graph, not the area.
Average velocity is total displacement divided by time, not directly the area.
cards.successCriteria: Student recognizes area under VT graph as displacement (vector), not distance.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Area under VT graph is a key concept in understanding linear motion.
cards.commonMisconception: Students think area under VT graph gives total distance traveled, ignoring sign/direction.

cards.question: The acceleration-time graph below shows constant positive acceleration. What does the area under the curve represent?
cards.diagnosis: Check if student confuses area with acceleration or final velocity.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
Acceleration is the y-axis value, not the area under the curve.
Area gives change in velocity (Δv), not final velocity. Final velocity requires initial velocity plus Δv.
Displacement is area under a velocity-time graph, not acceleration-time.
cards.successCriteria: Student identifies area under AT graph as change in velocity.
cards.ossdExpectation: Demonstrate an understanding of uniform and non-uniform linear motion, in one and two dimensions.
cards.alignmentNote: Understanding area under AT graph is essential for connecting acceleration to velocity change.
cards.commonMisconception: Students often think area under AT graph gives acceleration or final velocity instead of change in velocity.

cards.question: Two vectors are added using the tip-to-tail method. Which statement correctly describes the resultant vector?
options: The resultant is drawn from the tail of the first vector to the tip of the last vector.
The resultant is drawn from the tip of the first vector to the tail of the last vector.
The resultant is the sum of the magnitudes, ignoring direction.
The resultant is always the longest vector in the diagram.
cards.diagnosis: Check if student understands the tip-to-tail vector addition procedure.
misconceptions: ✓ 正确
That would not connect the starting point to the endpoint. The resultant must start at the initial point.
Vector addition takes direction into account; adding magnitudes only works if vectors are parallel and same direction.
The resultant can be shorter than the individual vectors if they partially cancel.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies that resultant is from tail of first to tip of last vector.
cards.ossdExpectation: Investigate uniform and non-uniform linear motion in qualitative and quantitative terms, and solve related problems.
cards.alignmentNote: Vector addition (tip-to-tail) is a key skill in solving problems related to motion.
cards.commonMisconception: Students sometimes think resultant goes from tip of first to tail of last or confuse the order.
